title: Where it grows
subtitle: A truly international grape
objectives: Explain how it adapts to different places

steps.title: Everywhere warm enough
steps.body: Cabernet's classic home is Bordeaux's Left Bank. It's the leading red in Napa Valley, Chile's Maipo, Australia's Coonawarra and Margaret River, Washington State and South Africa's Stellenbosch. In Italy it's key to Bolgheri's Super Tuscans. It also grows in Argentina, China and Spain.

steps.title: Needing warmth
steps.body: As a late ripener, Cabernet needs a long, warm season. In cool places it can taste green, from pyrazines that only break down when fully ripe. Warm, dry sites with well-drained soils suit it best. That's why it does so well on gravel and in sunny, irrigated New World regions.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Cabernet character.
steps.explanation: Place changes Cabernet's accent while its core stays.

steps.title: Why it travels well
steps.body: Cabernet's thick skins resist rot, its late budding avoids frost, and it keeps its character in many soils and climates. Growers find it reliable, and consumers recognise the name. That's how it became the world's most planted wine grape, overtaking others in the 1990s.

steps.prompt: Why can Cabernet taste green in cool climates?
options: Pyrazines that only break down with full ripeness
steps.explanation: Pyrazines give green pepper notes; full ripeness reduces them.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet grows in almost every wine country
It needs warmth and drainage to ripen fully
Its resistance and recognisability made it the most planted grape
